title: How to body measurements & discussing my weak points
summary: Introduces body measurements as an objective (but limited) progress marker, recommends a specific tape and measuring sparingly on fixed dates, and stresses bodybuilding isn't about measurements. He then rates his own body parts out of ten, explains which strong parts he can slack on, and lists his weak points (lats, upper traps, lateral/medial triceps, rear delts, calves, neck), launching a weak-point video series.

claims.claim: Measuring your muscles gives an objective criterion of progress and helps document what works and what doesn't in your training.
Muscle measurements are influenced by pump and body fat, not just hypertrophy; gaining 10% body fat raises all measurements without necessarily adding muscle.
He stays at the same bodyweight and body fat so his measurement gains reflect muscle; adding fat to boost measurements is pointless.
Use a self-tightening/locking body tape rather than a plain wrap-around tape, which can loosen and give ambiguous readings.
Beginners don't need to measure since they'll progress regardless, and taping can become an obsession, which is toxic.
He only measures one body part every two to three months to check for progress or regression.
If you measure, set fixed dates in advance (e.g. in six months) so you can't cheat, and document it.
Bodybuilding isn't about measurements: a guy with 22-inch arms can look worse than one with smaller arms because of insertions, arm length and posing.
A nice physique without posing skill is wasted talent.
He has clear, detailed physique goals rather than vague ones.
He rates his biceps 9/10, mid traps 8/10, quads 8/10 as his best body parts.
Past a certain point, objectively assess your body to know where you can 'slack off' so you can put more volume and effort into other body parts.
For quads he only squats; he has cut squat volume to pull more from the floor and hip hinge, and his legs are still growing because quads maintain while hamstrings grow.
He is biceps-obsessed but doesn't do much biceps volume; he focuses more on forearms and the brachialis, which are underdeveloped for him.
His mid traps grow from any pulling without being targeted.
His lower back and rhomboids are very developed (lower back 10/10); his rhomboids attach low so they grow from any pull, and a strong lower back makes his core bulletproof, so he keeps training it.
His triceps long head grows well and fast because he never targeted it before; naturals who neglect the long head will regret it, as he did.
His glutes look developed but much of it is fat; he stores a lot of fat there, so he gives credit to genetics rather than muscle.
Inner forearms, hamstrings, teres major/minor and abs are mid-tier for him.
His lats are a weak point because he only did pulls from the floor for years, a terrible idea; he now uses high volume and frequency to make them catch up.
His upper traps are a weak point, partly genetic; he started a strategy a week earlier that he hates but finds effective.

His lateral and medial triceps heads never grew despite much more work than the long head; he believes he trained them incorrectly, not bad genetics, and has found movements where he feels them strongly.
His rear delts and calves need work because he never really trained them; now that he does, they progress fine.
His neck looks fine relaxed but too skinny in a double biceps pose; he believes the neck should be about as big as the arms, so with 19-inch arms he wants at least an 18-inch neck.
